# Mobility Support

`customer_support.model.b2c.mobility` · vertical · parent `customer_support.model.b2c`

> Supporting ride-hailing, delivery, car-sharing and micromobility. The defining fact is that the customer is physically in the world while contacting us, and frequently stranded, stuck or unsafe. Support here is partly a real-time operations function: a rider left at the roadside at night is not a ticket with a response target, and a queue that answers them in four hours has failed regardless of what the SLA said. The second structural fact is that there are two customer populations with opposed interests in the same incident. A rider and a driver, or a customer and a courier, both contact us about the same trip with incompatible accounts of it, and support must adjudicate rather than serve. Every B2C service instinct — believe the customer, resolve in their favour, err toward goodwill — produces a systematically unfair outcome, because the other party is also our customer and is also right sometimes. Consistency of adjudication is the quality bar, and it is compared publicly. Third, a real subset of contacts are safety events: accidents, harassment, medical incidents, vehicle faults. These are not support tickets and must leave the support queue immediately for a specialist path with different training, different authority and legal obligations attached. A triage taxonomy that cannot separate a safety report from a fare dispute in the first seconds is a liability rather than a routing inconvenience. The error carried in from ecommerce is treating a disputed trip as a refund decision. It is a determination about two people's accounts, and refunding reflexively teaches one population that complaining is a fare discount.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a rider, driver, courier or customer who is physically mid-journey or has just finished one, contacting from a phone, often outdoors, often under time pressure and occasionally unsafe |
| typical_resolution_hours | 2 |
| volume_shape | tracks trip volume, so it peaks with commuting, weather and city events; weather-driven surges arrive with no warning and hit supply and demand simultaneously |
| staffing_model | large pooled real-time tier-1 with mandatory specialist paths for safety, insurance and claims; regional teams for local regulation and language |
| coverage | 24x7, with genuine urgency overnight because that is when stranded and safety contacts concentrate |
| automation_level | very high on fare, receipt and lost-item intents; hard-blocked on anything classified as safety, where automation is unacceptable |
| notes | Time-to-first-response has an unusually literal meaning here: for a stranded or unsafe contact it is not a service metric, it is the whole of the service.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `severity`, `priority`, `channel`, `intent_ref`


> Intent has to separate safety, stranded, dispute, fare and lost-item at intake, because they need different agents, different authority and different clocks — and because a safety report misrouted into a fare queue is the failure this vertical cannot afford. Severity here reads physical risk rather than system health.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `affected_user_ref`, `accessibility_needs`, `timezone`


> The two-population problem lives here. A trip has at least two requesters with opposed accounts, both of whom are our customers, and the object must be able to represent the counterparty rather than assuming a single asker.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `origin`, `reason_category`, `escalation_owner_ref`


> Safety and insurance escalations are not tier transfers, they are exits from the support process into a specialist function with legal obligations. The reason category is what makes that exit auditable rather than ad hoc.

> The claim most worth arguing with is emphasising quality_assurance over speed. In a real-time operation the pull is always toward faster handling, and consistency of adjudication loses every argument in the moment — but inconsistent rulings between two customers who can compare them is the failure that actually costs supply, and drivers compare rulings constantly.
